CPU EP InstanceNormalization<float> (used by both native and WASM builds; no WASM-specific kernel) computes per (n,c) channel: mean = Eigen Xi.mean(); variance is TWO-PASS: squared_norm = (Xi - mean).squaredNorm(); inv_stdev = 1.0f / std::sqrt(squared_norm / W + epsilon) (epsilon inside the sqrt, added to the variance); all in float (fp32) with no double accumulation; output Yi = Xi*channel_scale + (B - mean*channel_scale) where channel_scale = inv_stdev*scale (i.e. an algebraically folded affine, not (x-mean)*inv*scale+B).

claim: Because InstanceNorm uses Eigen reductions (mean(), squaredNorm()) and Eigen's summation order depends on the compile-time SIMD packet width, the fp32 rounding of mean/variance differs between builds with different Eigen vectorisation (native x64: SSE2/AVX packets and tree-reduction of lanes; WASM: whatever Eigen selects under emscripten, which as far as I know has no wasm-simd128 packet backend in Eigen 3.4, so it falls to scalar/sequential order). The ORT build only turns Eigen vectorisation off via option onnxruntime_DONT_VECTORIZE (EIGEN_DONT_VECTORIZE=1); I did not find it forced on for Emscripten in the files inspected. Exact per-build packet type NOT verified.

claim: CPU EP LayerNormalization<float> (layer_norm_impl.cc ComputeJob) FIRST tries MlasLayerNormF32(...); only if that returns false does it run the generic scalar fallback. The generic fallback uses Welford's ONE-PASS online algorithm in type T (float for fp32 models): delta=x-mean; mean += delta/(h+1); M2 += delta*(x-mean); std_dev = sqrt(M2/norm_size + epsilon) (epsilon added to variance inside the sqrt); output = (x-mean)/std_dev*scale + bias (a true divide by std_dev, not multiply by reciprocal), all in float.

claim: MlasLayerNormF32 returns false (=> fallback to Welford) when GetMlasPlatform().LayerNormF32Kernel is nullptr. On x86/AMD64 it also returns false if NormSize < 8 (LayerNorm) / < 16 (RMSNorm). The kernel pointer is assigned ONLY in platform.cpp for RISC-V RVV (L373) and x86 AVX2+FMA3 (L573 in the AMD64 AVX2 block; L718 for IX86). There is no assignment for WASM/Emscripten, so on ORT Web WASM LayerNormalization always takes the scalar Welford fallback, while native x64 with AVX2+FMA3 takes the AVX2 kernel (A-5).

claim: The native AVX2+FMA3 LayerNorm kernel differs numerically from the WASM/Welford path in three ways: (1) mean is a two-pass double-precision sum (vcvtps2pd+vaddpd, 4 lanes) then cast to float; (2) variance is a CENTERED TWO-PASS sum((x-mean)^2) accumulated in fp32 with 8-lane FMA (_mm256_fmadd_ps) and lane-tree horizontal reduction; (3) normalisation multiplies by inv_denom = 1.0f/sqrtf(var/n + eps) then by scale and uses FMA for the bias add (vy = fma(vy, scale, bias)), whereas the fallback divides by std_dev. Epsilon placement is the same (inside the sqrt, added to variance). So native and WASM LayerNorm are NOT bit-identical by construction; expected difference is a few fp32 ulps per element.

The session config key exists with the exact string "session.set_denormal_as_zero" (C constant kOrtSessionOptionsConfigSetDenormalAsZero). Value "1" enables flush-to-zero and denormal-as-zero; default "0". Header doc says: first session's setting applies to the main thread (and global OpenMP pool); threads in per-session thread pools follow each session's option; and 'turning this option on may hurt model accuracy'.

Native behaviour: InferenceSession reads the key (GetConfigOrDefault(..., "0") == "1") and, inside a process-wide std::call_once, calls SetDenormalAsZero(value) on the calling thread (so even with default "0" it ACTIVELY SETS FTZ/DAZ OFF on the main thread for the first session created in the process). Each intra/inter-op pool worker calls SetDenormalAsZero(set_denormal_as_zero_) at thread start. SetDenormalAsZero is implemented only for x86/x86_64 (needs SSE3 per CPUIDInfo): _MM_SET_DENORMALS_ZERO_MODE + _MM_SET_FLUSH_ZERO_MODE ON/OFF (MXCSR DAZ/FTZ bits), returns true; otherwise returns false and does nothing.

microsoft/onnxruntime PR #31973 'Add AVX2 LayerNorm/RMSNorm kernel for x86-64 (MLAS)' (state: merged, merge date reported as 2026-09-04) introduced the native x86 LayerNorm fast path. Select Chrome for Vitest 5.0.1 browser mode with playwright({launchOptions:{channel:'chrome', args:[...]}}). PlaywrightProviderOptions = { launchOptions (Playwright LaunchOptions minus tracesDir), connectOptions, contextOptions, actionTimeout, persistentContext }. The provider spreads providerOptions.launchOptions and then overwrites headless with the resolved browser.headless, so `headless` belongs in browser config, not launchOptions. `args` is the launch-args array (e.g. ['--enable-unsafe-webgpu']); per local spike no extra flags are needed for the Gen9 adapter.

Exact syntax. Global (all instances): `provider: playwright({ launchOptions: { channel: 'chrome' } })`. Per-instance override: give the instance its own `provider: playwright({...})`. Docs: per-instance provider options are NOT merged with the parent, they replace it, so repeat every launch option. The instances page lists no instance-level `launchOptions` key (documented: browser, headless, locators, viewport, testerHtmlPath, screenshotDirectory, screenshotFailures, provider). Installed Vitest allows an instance to carry its own provider but requires the same provider NAME/factory across all instances of a project. CONSEQUENCE for this repo: vitest.config.ts uses one global `playwright()` for chromium+firefox+webkit; putting channel:'chrome' there would also be passed to firefox/webkit launches. Two safe shapes: (i) per-instance `provider: playwright({launchOptions:{channel:'chrome'}})` on the chromium instance only, or (ii) a separate project (e.g. name 'browser-webgpu', include performance test only, instances:[{browser:'chromium'}], its own playwright({launchOptions:{channel:'chrome'}})). Shape (ii) is inferred to be the cleaner one because a project can also set its own `server.headers`/include; both are documented patterns.

claim: env.webgpu.profiling = { mode?: 'off'|'default' (default 'off'), ondata?: (data)=>void }. With mode 'default' and no ondata, per-kernel GPU timings are printed to the console with prefix '[profiling]' (logged as 'kernel ... start time: N ns, execution time: N ns'). If ondata is set it receives the data instead. Uses WebGPU timestamp queries: requires device feature 'timestamp-query' (or chromium-experimental-timestamp-query-inside-passes); if the adapter lacks it queryType stays 'none' and nothing is reported. Legacy env.webgpu.profilingMode is deprecated. Set before creating the session. Profiling adds overhead, so never use it in the runs that produce headline timings.

WebGPU shader compilation is lazy: a program's shader module + compute pipeline are built the first time a kernel with that (program, input-shape) key is dispatched, not at InferenceSession.create(); artifacts are then cached per key inside the backend. So the FIRST session.run() carries the compile/warm-up cost and later runs with identical input shapes reuse it. Chunks in this app are fixed-shape (1,2,343980), so run 2..N are steady state. Local measurement in SP-2 on the SP-2 reference (Gen9 4-core) machine agrees: WebGPU run 8.2 s (first) then 1.26 s (steady), create 48.3 s.

claim: With the default output location ('cpu'), `await session.run()` resolves only after the GPU work for that run has finished: the WASM-side output copy calls backend.download -> downloadGpuData, which encodes copyBufferToBuffer, flush()es (queue.submit) and `await gpuReadBuffer.mapAsync(GPUMapMode.READ)` before returning bytes. mapAsync resolves only after previously submitted queue work completes, so performance.now() before/after `await session.run(...)` is a valid wall-clock for the run including readback. Caveats: (1) this holds for cpu outputs only; with preferredOutputLocation:'gpu-buffer' (or graph capture) run() can resolve before GPU completion and would need an explicit sync/download; the app uses the default. (2) The number includes the readback/copy of the (1,4,2,343980) fp32 output, which is part of real cost. (3) No official doc states this contract; it is inferred from source, hence a spike check is listed in (b).

claim: Recommended WebGPU timing procedure (no official ORT warm-up doc exists: the ORT ep-webgpu, env-flags and performance-diagnosis pages contain no warm-up/first-run guidance). Derived from B-5/B-6: create the session once; perform >=1 untimed warm-up session.run with the SAME input shape (a real chunk or zeros of shape [1,2,343980]) and dispose its outputs; report three separate numbers: (i) download, (ii) session.create, (iii) first-run (cold) latency, then (iv) steady-state per-chunk = median of runs 2..N. Time each run individually with performance.now() around `await session.run()` plus reading `.data`. Extrapolate a 4-min song as first_run + (N-1) * steady, not N * mean(all). In a fresh browser profile there is no persistent shader/driver cache from earlier runs, so the cold first-run number is a realistic 'first visit' figure and a 'second visit' figure needs a relaunch of the same profile (see open questions).

claim: REPO FINDING (measurement bug that affects PERF.md): tests/browser/performance.test.ts sets modelLoadedAt at the FIRST 'separating' progress event with completed===1, i.e. AFTER chunk 1 has finished. 'model-ready' therefore includes download + session create + the entire first run (cold: WASM heap growth or WebGPU shader compile), and 'separation' (t1 - modelLoadedAt) covers only chunks 2..4 = 3 chunks. PERF.md divides that separation time by 4 ('per chunk 15.4 s' = 61.7/4; '26.3 s' = 105.0/4) and extrapolates 42 chunks, so per-chunk cost is UNDERSTATED by ~25% for that table (true steady-state per chunk from those numbers would be ~20.6 s for 3 threads and ~35.0 s for 1 thread, matching SP-2's 21.8 and 34.7 s/chunk much better) and the 4-min extrapolations (10.8 min / 18.4 min) are ~25% low (~14.4 and ~24.5 min at 42 chunks). The fix is to emit a progress/marker event after session creation (stage 'preparing-model' completed===1 already exists) and time each run separately.

claim: Benchmark methodology (2C/4T laptop). Supported points: (1) do not assume a steady state after a fixed number of warm-up iterations; a peer-reviewed study of VM benchmarks found only at most 43.5% of <VM, benchmark> pairs consistently reached steady state and recommends checking for it (changepoint analysis) rather than blindly discarding N iterations. (2) Repeat across separate process/browser launches, not only in-process iterations, because launch-to-launch variance (JIT/driver/thermal state) is not captured by in-process repeats. (3) Summarize with median and IQR (Tukey fences 1.5*IQR for outliers), not the mean. Concrete plan for this repo (inferred from these principles, not from a single authoritative source): >=5 fresh Playwright launches per config (WASM-3T, WASM-1T, WebGPU), each = 1 warm-up run (B-7) + >=5 timed chunks; report median and IQR of steady-state s/chunk, plus first-run and create times separately; alternate config order across launches (ABAB) to spread thermal drift; discard a launch only if its logged CPU frequency dropped (B-11) and say so; keep the machine on AC, lid open, no other heavy apps, same display state, and start each launch after CPU temperature/frequency is back to baseline (a 30-60 s idle gap; the exact value is a spike parameter).

claim: Recording CPU frequency/throttling on Windows: sample the perf counters with typeperf at 1 s during each run. Counters confirmed to exist on THIS machine via `typeperf -qx "Processor Information"`: \Processor Information(_Total)\Processor Frequency, \% of Maximum Frequency, \% Processor Performance, \% Performance Limit, \Performance Limit Flags (also % Processor Utility). Example: `typeperf "\Processor Information(_Total)\Processor Frequency" "\Processor Information(_Total)\% of Maximum Frequency" "\Processor Information(_Total)\% Processor Performance" "\Processor Information(_Total)\% Performance Limit" "\Processor Information(_Total)\Performance Limit Flags" -si 1 -f CSV -o freq.csv` (typeperf options: -si sample interval, -sc sample count, -f CSV|TSV|BIN|SQL, -o file, -cf counter file; Ctrl+C stops). Start it before the run and stop after; join to per-chunk timestamps. Throttling indicator: frequency (or % of Maximum Frequency) falling while CPU utilisation stays ~100%, or non-zero Performance Limit flags/% Performance Limit. Do NOT use Win32_Processor.CurrentClockSpeed/MaxClockSpeed: locally it reported 2300 / 2400 MHz (static-looking, MaxClockSpeed 2400 vs the SKU's 2.3 GHz base) and is not a live frequency. Interpretation of '% Processor Performance' relative to base frequency (can exceed 100 with turbo) comes from search summaries only.

claim: CDP throttling API and units. Network.emulateNetworkConditions {offline, latency (ms, 'minimum latency from request sent to response headers received'), downloadThroughput (bytes/sec, 'maximal AGGREGATED download throughput', -1 disables), uploadThroughput (bytes/sec, -1 disables), connectionType?}. It is marked DEPRECATED in the current protocol in favour of Network.emulateNetworkConditionsByRule (experimental; per-request urlPattern using URLPattern syntax, absolute patterns, first matching rule wins, empty pattern = global) plus Network.overrideNetworkState (navigator.onLine/connection). 50 Mbps = 50,000,000 / 8 = 6,250,000 bytes/sec (use 6.25e6, not 50*1024*1024/8 = 6,553,600 unless binary Mbit is intended). Because the by-rule form can target only the HF/CDN hosts, it avoids throttling the Vite dev-server assets; whether Chrome 154 accepts it must be checked (protocol JSON is 'master'). Playwright 1.63 has no native throttling API (only setOffline; feature request microsoft/playwright#32618 was open when read).

claim: How to reach CDP from a Vitest 5 browser test: `import { cdp } from 'vitest/browser'; const s = cdp(); await s.send('Network.enable'); await s.send('Network.emulateNetworkConditions', {offline:false, latency:L, downloadThroughput:6_250_000, uploadThroughput:-1})`. Vitest docs: works only with the playwright provider and chromium, and (per docs summary) needs the API write/exec permissions in config (api.allowWrite / api.allowExec) - verify the exact keys against 5.0.1 before relying on them. Alternative that avoids that permission: register a server-side command with defineBrowserCommand (exported by @vitest/browser-playwright) whose context exposes { page, context } (getCommandsContext), then call `context.newCDPSession(page)` and send the same commands; the page CDPSession is the documented Playwright route (Chromium only). The CDP session is per page target and throttling state must be removed (-1/0) or the context closed after the test.

claim: Does Network.emulateNetworkConditions apply to the app's model download? (a) Requests from the page/frames on the CDP-attached page target: yes, this is the mechanism DevTools presets use (multiple practitioner posts; Puppeteer docs). (b) Service-worker-initiated fetches: NOT throttled (Puppeteer #4305: page request 1,421 ms vs SW request 38 ms under Slow 3G; closed with no documented fix). (c) Dedicated Web Worker fetches (the production path: separate() runs in src/worker.ts and getModel/fetch runs there): NO authoritative source found either way. Playwright's own code skips worker sessions when issuing Network.emulateNetworkConditions, and a search summary claimed 'workers are affected by the owner frame's emulation', but neither is a maintainer statement about throttling. (d) Cross-origin redirects (HF /resolve/ URL -> CDN host): no source found; the protocol says latency is per request and throughput is 'aggregated', and DevTools throttling operates at the network layer for the page, so redirects are expected to be covered, but this is unverified. (e) Puppeteer docs: emulation does not affect WebSockets/WebRTC (crbug 563644), irrelevant to fetch(). Consequence: the existing perf test calls separate() on the test-page main thread (not the worker) so (a) applies; a measurement through the real UI/worker path must be verified by a spike.

claim: Cold Cache API in a fresh context. Playwright BrowserContexts are 'equivalent to incognito-like profiles' with their own storage, and Vitest 5.0.1's provider does `this.persistentContext ?? await browser.newContext(options)`; persistentContext defaults to false, so each Vitest browser session starts with an empty Cache Storage and empty HTTP cache. Guard against reuse: leave persistentContext off (it is off in vitest.config.ts); ONE Vitest session/context is shared by all test files of that instance, so a prior test in the same run that calls getModel() will already have populated Cache Storage - either run the download test first/alone, or delete the entry: `await caches.delete(<CACHE_NAME from src/model/cache.ts>)` (cache.ts opens caches.open(CACHE_NAME) and cache.match(info.url)) and also assert `!(await cache.match(url))` before timing. HTTP cache: use Network.setCacheDisabled {cacheDisabled:true} (protocol: 'cache will not be used') or Network.clearBrowserCache, or fetch(..., {cache:'no-store'}) for the timed download; a fresh incognito context already has an empty HTTP cache.
